Messages.Author: Damnans
Messages.Body:
V:EKN Tournament Rules
2004 Season (Mid-Season Update)
Effective July 1, 2004

http://www.white-wolf.com/vtes/veknRules200407.html

[...]

Changes from the January 1, 2004 rules

2.9 Removed maximum number of participants to allow use of Multi-Judge
System in most events.
3.1.5 Multi-Deck option added for small tournaments.
3.1.6 Added "No Final Round" option for small tournaments.

2.9. Multi-Judge System

The Multi-Judge System may be used at any non-qualifier,
non-championship tournament with at least eight participants
(i.e., having at least two tables). Organizers choosing
this system must announce its use before the tournament
begins and identify six judges as head judge, secondary
judge, and third, fourth, fifth, and sixth judge. Organizers
should use good judgement when selecting the Multi-Judge
System and should ensure its use will not disrupt the event.
Tournament organizers may only participate in events they
sanction if they are using the Multi-Judge System. These
types of events are the only ones in which judges and/or
tournament organizers are allowed to participate.

When using the Multi-Judge System, the head judge makes all
rulings, except when a decision is needed in a game in which
the head judge is participating. If a ruling is needed in a
head judge's game, the secondary judge makes the call, except
in games in which both the head judge and secondary judge are
both participating, and so on. The only time the sixth judge
makes a ruling is when the head judge, the secondary judge,
and the third, fourth, and fifth judges are playing a game.

3.1.5 Multi-Deck System

Players are prohibited from making modifications to their
decks between rounds unless the tournament uses the following
multi-deck rules. The multi-deck system can be used at any
tournament with fewer than 12 players (i.e., fewer than three
tables). Organizers choosing to use this system must announce
its use in advance of the tournament date. Players may choose
to bring any number of tournament-legal decks to the tournament
and/or extra cards to exchange with cards in their decks (also
known as a sideboard in some games). Between rounds, players
may freely switch decks (or cards in their decks). A tournament
begun with the multi-deck system cannot admit more players
between rounds if doing so would create a round with 12 or more
players.

3.1.6 Tournament Without Final

In a very small tournament, one with fewer than 8 players
(i.e., fewer than two tables), the organizer may choose to omit
the final round altogether or may choose to run an additional
"preliminary" round in place of the final. This decision must
be made and announced to all the players prior to the start of
the first round. With no final, the results of the preliminary
rounds (including the additional preliminary round, if any) are
used to determine final standings in the same manner as
described in 3.1 above. The no-final rules can be used in
conjunction with or without the multi-deck system above, at the
organizer's option. A tournament begun under the no-final
arrangement cannot admit more players between rounds if doing
so would create a round with 8 or more players.

Greetings,
Damnans

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
Reyda wrote:

> what do you think ?

I think in a tournament with people playing one deck the whole time (i.e. a
standard tournament), it is a bad idea, as it:

-Makes overpowered hoser cards too attractive (if you know that someone is
doing really well with a Malkavian deck, you put a whole bunch of Dementias
in your deck).

-Makes scouting too attractive (if you know what everyone else is playing,
you can change your deck as necessary, so having extra information becomes
huge).

-Is useless in most cases anyway, as you have zero way to know what you are
going tobe sitting next to (unless you are suggesting that you get to
"sideboard" *after* you see where you are at a table. Which is insane.)

In the situation it exists in now, where people can play completely
different decks between rounds, it is hardly an issue, as there will tend to
be very little consistiently between rounds. Mostly it'll be good for
tweaking a deck you are working on as you play, and making it work better in
general after playing it a few times.

Personally, I'd be very much against this.

One of the biggest challenges in deckbuilding is the limited amount of
cards you have to include in the deck - the 90-card limit forces you
to make decisions about what to include, because you can't include
everything to cover every contingency.

It also would give a HUGE advantage to players who either a) finish
their games really fast or b) have friends helping them scout other
decks. Players whose games were timing out would be at a distinct
disadvantage in knowing what cards would be ideal to sideboard for
their next game as opposed to the player whose game finished in an
hour and spent the rest walking around observing games and decks.

Based on what I've observed from other CCG's tournaments, sideboarding
would not be an issue of 'my deck isn't playing right for the
environment' or thoughts of 'today I feel like being more agressive'.
Instead, it's much much much more likely to be specifically used to
swap in and out cards to combat the decks you're about to immediately
face.

For instance, you might swap in 3 weenie DOM vamps and 10 deflections
if you know a weenie bleed deck is about to be at your table, or swap
out PTOs from your vote deck if you're going to be at an all-Cam
table, or swap in a couple of Anachronisms or Illegal Search+Seizures
if you know an Assault Rifle deck's coming. Non-combat decks coming?
Quick, swap in the War Ghouls. (Plus, fourteen cards is a LOT. Other
games have had very, very small sideboards, to prevent people from
playing what is effectively a very different deck each round - I'd bet
with a fourteen-of-ninety swap, you could build some decks that played
VERY differently, like swapping an entire discipline's worth of cards
through your deck.)

And while letting everybody sideboard is certainly something that
players can feasibly do, it's not what I would personally want to see
as the official default tournament rule. I _like_ getting to play the
meta-game of figuring out in advance what sorts of decks I'm likely to
see at a tourney and whether/how to account for them in my
deckbuilding, because I won't be able to swap things in and out once
the tourney starts.

It could make for an interesting alternate format, certainly - it's
just not one I'd want to play as the default, at all.

-John Flournoy

John Flournoy wrote:

> Based on what I've observed from other CCG's tournaments, sideboarding

> Instead, it's much much much more likely to be specifically used to
> swap in and out cards to combat the decks you're about to immediately

Frome what I understand, in Magic, you have a "base" deck that you always
play your first game against a given opponent in a given match of 3 games
with, and then after the first game, you can sideboard in cards, resetting
your deck to "base" after the three game match.

This makes perfect sense--you play one game against one player, see what you
are playing against, and adjust accordingly.

VTES does not have this system even remotely, and as such, sideboarding is
both totally random and likely pointless.

Again, in the "multi deck" format, you aren't so much "sideboarding" between
rounds as you are just using a different deck every round. Which works fine,
as everyone is doing the same thing, theoretically. Having a "sideboard" for
a single deck in a single tournament has the possibility of being
preposterously overpowered, and at the same time, mostly pointless.

I think it depends on the point of registering decks. Usually, the reason
to do so is to prove that a player has played the same deck throughout
the tournament - e.g., hasn't added three Malkavian Dementias to his deck
just because he's discovered the field is swarming with Malk decks.
Obvioiusly, in a tournament with such rules, any need for that becomes
obviated.

If you simply want to see to it that the decks played are legal, that can
be done without registering decks. A simple deck check would suffice.
Of course, in a tournament where decks can change each round rather than
having one deck for the whole tournament, that would admittedly be more
of a pain.

Fred

Messages.Body:

> Well i hope there are no plans to expand this idea to larger tournaments. I
> can just see if now, someone that has not gotten any VP in the first 2

> just random rush combat or their "funny reseat the table every time its my

That sounds like a bit of a straw man issue to me. I'd never say never,
as there are always a few jerks and morons out there. But I don't think
that's likely to be much of a problem, if I understand what you mean.

What might be more of an issue (and maybe this is more what you were
talking about and I'm just misunderstanding), are people playing kinds
of "extreme" decks that you'd normally never see in a serious tournament.
For instance, I have a deck with a ton of Kiss of Ras in it, built to
gamble that there will be little or no fortitude at the table. If I
play it and most of the vampires at the table have fortitude, I just
basically starve and die. Such a deck would have a very random
influence on the game, which other players might find annoying.

If this is what you're concerned about, I'd say that I sympathize with
the point of view. (No one wants to miss out on the finals because their
grandprey "ally" brought out a deck that died horribly to their prey.)
But some might see such a rule as a *good* thing - exactly because it
would give a player doing poorly an opportunity to use a gadget or
extreme deck in the last round. This, in turn, would force others to
consider the possibilities when evaluating the metagame. Bottom line:
I think it should be the choice of tournament director, not a set rule
concerning the size of the tournament. That would also settle questions
about knowing whether the multiple-deck rule would be used or not
depending on how many people show up.

Messages.Author: Frederick Scott
Messages.Body:
RavATwoFaces wrote:
> > 3.1.5 Multi-Deck System
> >
> > Players are prohibited from making modifications to their
> > decks between rounds unless the tournament uses the following
> > multi-deck rules. The multi-deck system can be used at any
> > tournament with fewer than 12 players (i.e., fewer than three
> > tables). Organizers choosing to use this system must announce
> > its use in advance of the tournament date. Players may choose
> > to bring any number of tournament-legal decks to the tournament
> > and/or extra cards to exchange with cards in their decks (also
> > known as a sideboard in some games). Between rounds, players
> > may freely switch decks (or cards in their decks). A tournament
> > begun with the multi-deck system cannot admit more players
> > between rounds if doing so would create a round with 12 or more
> > players.
> >
>
> This is the weird new rule I've seen in years (and I'm a Malkavian...)
> Sideboard or deck swapping?
> I think it's ok but with limitations.
>
> It' not good to have player who behaves in the following way:
> "I've 12 decks ready and I'll take all my card collection to the
> tournment..."

You can take every card you own but you can only play three. In this
sense, owning more cards or more decks isn't the slightest advantage.
You may be able to switch decks - but so can everyone else! So you
know nothing about what anyone else can play. Therefore, the ability
to switch to large number of different decks is totally meaningless.
For the most part, you might as well plan your three (or four or whatever)
decks in advance. The only reason not to I can think of is if you want
to choose a deck based on your position in the tournament so far (that is,
whether you're pretty much in the finals already or haven't scored at all
or you're on the cusp of making it into the finals). The other reason
I can think of would be if you saw some type or types of decks in
abundance that you hadn't expected, for instance a ton of combat decks
when you were expecting bleed decks. Even so, basing your choice on
that seems very risky to me. The next round may see everyone swap out
their combat decks.

This is a poor objection to the multi-deck rule, IMHO.

> Instead I think that a "limited" sideboard (say as 20 card and a
> maximum of 5 vamps to exchange 1:1 in the deck) is a good choice and
> also a "second deck"... no more.

I agree with the people who think sideboarding is a bad idea. It
would encourage scouting, which is a bad thing. The current rule is
much better.

> > 3.1.6 Tournament Without Final
> >
> > In a very small tournament, one with fewer than 8 players
> > (i.e., fewer than two tables), the organizer may choose to omit
> > the final round altogether or may choose to run an additional
> > "preliminary" round in place of the final.
>
> Agreed, it make non sense to have a final...
> Last month I've attended a tournment with 5 players + judge.
> A single round will be enough!

Why not have two or three rounds, if you have time? (And use
the multi-deck system, which were included first and foremost for
exactly this situation.) This is like saying a single game is
enough for a pickup play night. Finals or not, more is better.

Fred

with prizes and rankngs and a sense of "event", rather than just getting
together to play some pick up games, people show up, people bring decks that
are winners, rather than just experimental, and everyone enjoys the
eventiness of it. Yeah, someone or someones get prizes. Everyone gets some
promo cards. We usually get a big box of coffee for everyone to share.
Someone gets a free door prize (like, a booster or somethng that gets chosen
randomly). But this would happen with a 5 person tournament just as well as
it would with a 12 person tournament. And that there were only 5 people

like, 5 minutes to send a tournament report to Robin. It takes a bit longer
to post a winning deck, but you really only need to that if A) you want to

tournament, and you get some prizes and you play on having an event, if for
whatever reason, you only get 5 people, you still might as well have the
event, and it is still going to be a good time. Someone wins some free
stuff. Someone gets to mock their opponents with their victory. Everyone
gets some rating points.

As mentioned before, yeah, 2 tables is better than 1 table, and 3 tables is
evern better. But if you have planned an event, and you only got 5 guys, it
is good that the tournament rules are now structured to make this work

No, I'm not all that interested in prizes.
...

> If you think tournaments are more competitive for whatever reason and
> prefer a more competitive level of play, why can't that be achieved in
> nontournament play? Some people already have a similarity between the
> two.

It's just not the same thing. And as I say this, I will say that I
certainly think both ways of playing a set of games (keeping score and
calling it a "tournament" or not) have merit. But most people will not
treat it the same way - and I'm one of them. It's like the difference
between playing a single hand of hearts and keeping score up to 100, or
200, or 500, or whatever. The objective is no longer a single hand but
a result that represent an entire afternoon.

I also think there'a a shared expectation amongst most participants
that the competition level is higher during a tournament, that people
should care more whether they win or not. Like you, I don't exactly
agree with attitude. But then, like most people I need chances to try
my experimental decks so I'll generally do it at other times besides
tournaments. By the same token, I also find it good to have the
tournament times because then I know the competition will be tougher
and I can get better information about how good a deck really is that's
done well in pick-up play. If I can win with a deck in a tournament,
it's less likely that it only happened because my prey was playing some
whack deck and all of it's flaws came out at the critical moments and made
him fall over for me.

> Though, what I did say was "officially cancel". Can still run the
> tournament for the players, just don't have to bother with making
> sure you follow certain rules or filling out The Archon.

When you call a tournament, I find it - and I think others find it -
disappointing not to have an event that follows that particular format.
That's what people showed up for. Of course, you can keep tournament
scoring without the Archon, but why? I agree with Peter - it's trivial
stuff. And if I'm correct that not having a tournament when you've
scheduled one disappoints people, then a corollary would be that those
people will be less like to show up at the next tournament, thus possibly
causing the next one to fall through too.

I have a friend who teaches private classes in something she happens to
be good at. She advertises the classes and if even one student shows up,
she'll hold the class even though it's just a one-on-one tutoring session.
It's a terrible deal for her but I guess she feels that the intergrity of
it is important to her ability to attract future students. I suspect the
same is probably true for tournaments, too.

> While it never came up as to why we believe single rounds are enough
> in this thread, I've mentioned before, somewhere, how I've played
> multiround, single table tournaments and just how inane it was. What
> reason do you have to play more than one round?

You're the one who's positing that it's inane to play them. You tell me.
For my part, I see people playing more games of Jyhad than one, which is
the same reason I try to play as many games of Jyhad during a pickup night
as I can. What reason do you have to play only one round? For that matter,
what's different about a multi-table Jyhad tournament that we can't also
call it "inane" to play more than one round of THAT also? Bottom: you've
failed to state why you think it's "inane" to play more than one round
in a single-table tournament. Clarify that and I'll give my reason(s) for
disagreeing with it (assuming I do, of course).

> Do you really think it's any fairer? That people won't pound the crap
> out of the tournament leader because if they don't, that player will
> just win based on earlier success?

I guess I don't think it's that easy to necessarily do. I mean, why don't
they pound the crap out of the guy who's winning the first game DURING
the first game, for that matter? And if they do it later, what of it?
Pounding the crap out of the leader is part of the charm of multiplayer
gaming.

Again, consider the comparison with Hearts. Someone wins the first hand,
you play others. You pound the crap out the early leader if and when you
can. Sometimes he wins anyway. It's a system that seems to work well
enough. I just don't see the issue you're raising.

Fred
